goals: Define biotechnology and state its two core techniques
Explain how restriction enzymes are named and how they cut DNA
Describe gel electrophoresis and the features of a cloning vector
Explain how host cells are made competent to take up DNA

slides.heading: Biotechnology: Principles and Processes
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the principles of biotechnology and the molecular tools used to cut, join and move genes.

nodes.label: Genetic engineering: change the genetic material
Bioprocess engineering: grow cells in sterile conditions

visual.alt: Flow showing genetic engineering and bioprocess engineering leading to useful products

slides.narration: Biotechnology uses living organisms, or parts of them, to make products useful to people. The European Federation of Biotechnology describes it as the integration of natural science and organisms, cells, their parts and molecular analogues for products and services. Two techniques make modern biotechnology possible: genetic engineering and bioprocess engineering.

slides.heading: The two core techniques
slides.body_md: **Genetic engineering** alters the chemistry of genetic material (DNA and RNA) and introduces it into host organisms, changing their phenotype. **Bioprocess engineering** maintains a **sterile (microbial-contamination-free)** ambience to grow only the desired microbe or cell in large quantities.

rows: Create recombinant DNA and introduce it into a host
Grow the host in large numbers in sterile conditions to make a product

visual.alt: Table of the two core techniques of modern biotechnology

slides.narration: Traditional breeding mixes thousands of genes at once and can carry unwanted ones along. Genetic engineering lets scientists isolate just the gene they want and put it into another organism. Bioprocess engineering then grows that organism on a large scale, free of contamination, to collect the product.

slides.heading: The first recombinant DNA
slides.body_md: In **1972**, **Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer** made the first recombinant DNA: they cut out an **antibiotic-resistance gene** and linked it to a **native plasmid** of *Salmonella typhimurium*, then transferred it into ***Escherichia coli***. The DNA could multiply because it was linked to an **origin of replication (ori)**.

nodes.label: Maintain it in the host and pass it to progeny

visual.alt: Flow of the three basic steps in genetically modifying an organism

slides.narration: A piece of foreign DNA cannot multiply on its own inside a cell. It must be joined to a DNA molecule that has an origin of replication, such as a plasmid. A plasmid is a small circle of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main chromosome, that copies itself. Joined to it, the foreign gene is copied too.

slides.heading: Restriction enzymes: molecular scissors
slides.body_md: In **1963**, two enzymes responsible for restricting the growth of bacteriophage in *E. coli* were isolated: one added methyl groups to DNA, the other **cut DNA** — a **restriction endonuclease**. The first, **Hind II**, always cut DNA at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of **six base pairs**: its **recognition sequence**. Today more than **900** restriction enzymes from over **230** strains of bacteria are known.

rows: First enzyme isolated from this strain (order of isolation)

visual.alt: Table explaining the parts of the name EcoRI

slides.narration: Restriction enzymes belong to a larger group called nucleases. Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA; endonucleases cut at specific positions inside it. Each restriction endonuclease recognises its own short sequence. Their names follow a simple code, as shown for EcoRI.

slides.heading: Palindromes and sticky ends
slides.body_md: Each restriction endonuclease recognises a **palindromic** sequence — one that reads the **same 5′ → 3′ on both strands**. Many cut the two strands a little away from the centre, between the same two bases, leaving **single-stranded overhangs** called **sticky ends**.

slides.narration: Read the top strand of the EcoRI site from five prime to three prime: G A A T T C. Now read the bottom strand, also five prime to three prime: G A A T T C again. That is a DNA palindrome. EcoRI cuts both strands between G and A, so each fragment is left with a short single-stranded tail, a sticky end, that can pair with a matching tail.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: palindrome or not?
slides.body_md: Which of these could be recognition sites (palindromes)? A sequence is palindromic if it equals its reverse complement.
bullets: GAATTC → reverse complement GAATTC → **palindrome**
GGATCC → reverse complement GGATCC → **palindrome**
GAATTG → reverse complement CAATTC → **not a palindrome**
AAGCTT → reverse complement AAGCTT → **palindrome**

visual.alt: Worked table testing four sequences for palindromes

slides.narration: To test a sequence, write its complement, then read it backwards so that it also runs five prime to three prime. If you get the original sequence back, it is a palindrome. G A A T T C, G G A T C C and A A G C T T pass this test; G A A T T G does not.

slides.heading: Why sticky ends matter
slides.body_md: When the vector and the source DNA are cut with the **same restriction enzyme**, the fragments have **matching sticky ends**. These pair by hydrogen bonds and are sealed by **DNA ligase**, forming **recombinant DNA**.

nodes.label: Cut source DNA and vector with the same enzyme

visual.alt: Flow of making recombinant DNA using one restriction enzyme and DNA ligase

slides.narration: This is the key trick of genetic engineering. Using the same enzyme on both pieces of DNA guarantees that their sticky ends match. They stick together, and DNA ligase joins their sugar-phosphate backbones permanently, making a single recombinant molecule.

slides.body_md: DNA fragments are separated in **agarose gel** (agarose is extracted from seaweed). DNA is **negatively charged**, so in an electric field it moves towards the **anode**. The gel acts as a sieve: **smaller fragments move farther**.

slides.narration: DNA samples are loaded into wells at the negative end. When current flows, the fragments move towards the positive end, the small ones slipping through the gel faster. The DNA is stained with ethidium bromide and seen as bright orange bands under ultraviolet light. A band can then be cut out and its DNA extracted, which is called elution.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how many fragments?
slides.body_md: (a) The DNA strand 5′–TTACGGAATTCTTAGCGAATTCAAGT–3′ is cut with EcoRI (GAATTC, cut between G and A). How many fragments form? (b) In random DNA, a six-base site occurs about once in 4⁶ bases. About how many EcoRI sites are expected in 20480 bp?
bullets: (a) The site occurs 2 times, so the strand is cut into **3 fragments**: TTACGG | AATTCTTAGCG | AATTCAAGT.
So a gel of the digest would show bands at the expected fragment sizes.

visual.alt: Worked table: 3 fragments; about 5 sites expected

slides.narration: Each occurrence of the site is one cut, and every cut adds one fragment, so two sites give three fragments. For the second part, there are four bases, so a particular six-base sequence turns up on average once every four to the power six, four thousand and ninety-six, bases. Twenty thousand four hundred and eighty bases would hold about five sites.

slides.narration: This map shows pBR322. It has an origin of replication, two antibiotic-resistance genes for ampicillin and tetracycline, a rop gene that helps control copy number, and recognition sites for several restriction enzymes. Some of these sites lie inside the resistance genes, which is very useful, as we will see.

slides.heading: Features a cloning vector needs
slides.body_md: A good vector has four features.

rows: Starts replication; controls copy number of linked DNA
Identifies transformants; usually antibiotic resistance (ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, kanamycin)
Very few, preferably single, recognition sites for common enzymes, so the vector is cut only once
Easier to handle and to take up

visual.alt: Table of the features of a cloning vector and why each is needed

slides.narration: The origin lets the vector, and anything joined to it, be copied many times. A selectable marker, usually an antibiotic-resistance gene, lets us pick out cells that took up the vector. A single cloning site for an enzyme means the vector is cut in one place only, so the foreign DNA goes in neatly.

slides.heading: Insertional inactivation: finding recombinants
slides.body_md: Inserting foreign DNA **into a marker gene** inactivates it: **insertional inactivation**. If DNA is inserted at the **BamHI** site in the **tetracycline-resistance** gene of pBR322, recombinants **lose tetracycline resistance** but keep ampicillin resistance.

visual.alt: Table of growth of untransformed, non-recombinant and recombinant cells on ampicillin and tetracycline

slides.narration: Plate the cells on ampicillin first: only those with a plasmid grow. Then copy the colonies onto tetracycline. Those that fail to grow on tetracycline must carry an insert in the tetracycline gene, so they are recombinants. A simpler alternative uses the gene for beta-galactosidase: with a coloured substrate, non-recombinant colonies turn blue, while recombinants with an inactivated gene stay white.

slides.heading: Vectors for plants and animals; competent hosts
slides.body_md: ***Agrobacterium tumefaciens*** naturally delivers a piece of DNA (T-DNA) into plant cells; its **Ti plasmid** is modified into a **disarmed** cloning vector. **Retroviruses** are disarmed to carry genes into animal cells. DNA is **hydrophilic** and cannot pass through cell membranes, so host cells are made **competent**.

rows: Bacterial cells treated with calcium, incubated on ice with DNA, heated briefly to 42 °C, then put back on ice
DNA injected directly into the nucleus of an animal cell
Plant cells bombarded with high-velocity gold or tungsten microparticles coated with DNA
Infect the cell and transfer the recombinant DNA

visual.alt: Table of methods for introducing DNA into host cells

slides.narration: Bacteria do not normally take up DNA, so they are made competent. Calcium increases the efficiency with which DNA enters through pores in the cell wall, and a brief heat shock helps. Animal cells can have DNA injected straight into the nucleus. Plant cells can be shot with tiny DNA-coated metal particles from a gene gun.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Biotechnology: genetic engineering + bioprocess engineering (sterile ambience). First recombinant DNA: Cohen and Boyer (1972).
Restriction endonucleases recognise palindromic sequences; EcoRI = Escherichia coli, strain RY 13, first enzyme; sticky ends; DNA ligase joins.
Gel electrophoresis: agarose; DNA moves to the anode; smaller fragments farther; ethidium bromide and UV; elution.
Vectors: ori, selectable marker, single cloning sites, small size; pBR322 (ampR, tetR); insertional inactivation; blue-white selection.
Plant and animal vectors: disarmed Ti plasmid, retroviruses. Competence: calcium and heat shock; micro-injection; biolistics.

visual.alt: Summary table of the tools of recombinant DNA technology

slides.narration: To recap: restriction enzymes cut DNA at palindromic sites, leaving sticky ends that ligase can join. Gel electrophoresis separates fragments by size. Vectors such as pBR322 carry the gene into a host and let us select recombinants, and hosts are made competent to take up the DNA.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Explain each letter of **EcoRI**.
Show a **palindrome** by writing both strands 5′→3′.
State why DNA moves to the **anode** and why **small fragments travel farther**.

slides.narration: Exam tips. Be able to decode EcoRI. Show a palindrome by reading both strands five prime to three prime. Explain the movement of DNA in a gel. And explain insertional inactivation using which antibiotics recombinants can and cannot grow on.

slides.heading: Processes of recombinant DNA technology
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the steps from extracting DNA to making a finished product.

visual.alt: Flow of the steps of recombinant DNA technology

slides.narration: Recombinant DNA technology follows a sequence of steps: isolate the DNA, cut it, amplify the gene of interest, join it into a vector, put it into a host, grow the host, and finally purify the product. Let us go through each step.

slides.heading: Step 1: isolating DNA
slides.body_md: DNA is enclosed in membranes, so the cell must be broken open. Then other macromolecules are removed, and DNA is precipitated.

rows: Add chilled ethanol: DNA precipitates as fine threads (spooling)

visual.alt: Table of treatments used to isolate pure DNA

slides.narration: Different cells need different enzymes to open them: lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plants, and chitinase for fungi. The released mixture contains RNA, proteins and fats, so ribonuclease and protease remove RNA and proteins. Finally, chilled ethanol makes the purified DNA come out of solution as fine white threads, which can be spooled onto a rod.

slides.heading: Step 2: cutting DNA
slides.body_md: Purified DNA is incubated with a **restriction enzyme** under optimal conditions. **Agarose gel electrophoresis** checks the progress of digestion. The **vector** is cut with the **same enzyme**, and the gene of interest is joined to it.

nodes.label: Cut vector with the same enzyme

visual.alt: Flow of cutting source DNA and vector with the same enzyme and joining them

slides.narration: Cutting is checked on a gel: uncut DNA stays as one large band, while digested DNA gives smaller fragments. The vector is opened with the same enzyme, so its sticky ends match those of the gene, and the two can be joined.

slides.heading: Step 3: amplifying the gene by PCR
slides.body_md: **PCR (polymerase chain reaction)** makes many copies of a gene in a test tube. It uses **two primers** (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to the ends of the target region) and a **thermostable DNA polymerase** from the bacterium ***Thermus aquaticus*** (**Taq** polymerase).

slides.narration: In each cycle, heat separates the two DNA strands, the mixture cools so that primers bind to the ends of the target, and Taq polymerase builds new strands from the primers. Taq polymerase survives the high temperature of the denaturing step because it comes from a bacterium that lives in hot springs. Every cycle doubles the copies.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: how many copies?
slides.body_md: Starting from one DNA molecule, how many copies of the target are there after 10 cycles and after 30 cycles of PCR, assuming perfect doubling?
bullets: Rule — copies after $n$ cycles $= 2^n$.
After 30 cycles: $2^{30} = 1073741824 \approx 1.07 \times 10^{9}$ — about a billion copies.

visual.alt: Worked table: copies after 1, 5, 10, 20 and 30 cycles, reaching 1073741824

slides.narration: Doubling is powerful. Ten cycles turn one molecule into one thousand and twenty-four. Thirty cycles give more than a billion copies, enough to study a gene from a tiny sample. That is why PCR is used in research, in diagnosing infections and in forensic science.

slides.body_md: Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about the temperature of the denaturation step.

slides.heading: Step 4: ligation and step 5: transformation
slides.body_md: The gene is joined to the cut vector by **DNA ligase**, making a **recombinant DNA** molecule. This is introduced into competent host cells (**transformation**). Host cells are then grown on a medium containing the antibiotic for which the vector carries resistance, so that **only transformants survive**.

rows: Gene inserted into vector; ligase seals joints
Recombinant DNA enters competent host cells

visual.alt: Table of ligation, transformation and selection

slides.narration: Not every cell takes up the plasmid, so selection is essential. If the vector carries a gene for ampicillin resistance, only cells that took up the vector can grow on an ampicillin plate. Insertional inactivation or blue-white screening then tells recombinants from non-recombinants.

slides.heading: Step 6: obtaining the foreign gene product
slides.body_md: When the inserted gene is expressed in the host, the host makes a **recombinant protein**. To get large amounts, cells are grown in **continuous culture**: used medium is drained from one side while fresh medium is added from the other, keeping cells in their most active **log (exponential) phase**.

visual.alt: Flow from recombinant cells through continuous culture to a large yield of protein

slides.narration: A small flask gives only a small amount of product. Continuous culture keeps the cells growing at their fastest rate for a long time, which gives more biomass and more of the desired protein. For industrial scale, large vessels called bioreactors are used.

slides.heading: Bioreactors
slides.body_md: **Bioreactors** are large vessels (often **100–1000 litres**) in which raw materials are converted by microbes, plant, animal or human cells into specific products. They provide **optimal conditions**: temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins and oxygen. The **stirred-tank** type is the most common.

rows: Separate the product from cells and medium

slides.narration: The broth from a bioreactor contains cells, leftover nutrients and many other molecules. The product has to be separated and purified, then formulated with preservatives. Medicines must also pass clinical trials and strict quality control. These steps differ from product to product.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: planning a project
slides.body_md: A company wants bacteria to make a human protein. Put these steps in order and name the key tool or reagent for each: transform E. coli; amplify the human gene; purify the protein; cut gene and plasmid; grow cells in a bioreactor; join gene to plasmid; select transformants.

2. **Cut** gene and plasmid — the same restriction enzyme.
3. **Join** — DNA ligase.
4. **Transform** E. coli — calcium treatment and heat shock.
5. **Select** transformants — antibiotic medium (and blue-white screening).
6–7. **Grow** in a stirred-tank bioreactor, then **purify** by downstream processing.

notes.title: Biotechnology: Principles and Processes — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Principles of biotechnology
sections.body_md:
**Biotechnology** (European Federation of Biotechnology): the integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof and molecular analogues for products and services. Two core techniques:
- **Genetic engineering:** altering the chemistry of genetic material (DNA/RNA) and introducing it into host organisms to change their phenotype.
- **Bioprocess engineering:** maintaining a sterile (microbial-contamination-free) ambience in chemical engineering processes so that only the desired microbe or eukaryotic cell grows, in large quantities.

Traditional hybridisation may carry undesirable genes along with desired ones; genetic engineering transfers only the desired genes.

**First recombinant DNA (1972):** **Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer** linked an antibiotic-resistance gene to a native plasmid of *Salmonella typhimurium* and transferred it into *E. coli*. A piece of DNA can multiply only when linked to an **origin of replication (ori)**.

**Three basic steps:** (1) identify DNA with desirable genes; (2) introduce it into the host; (3) maintain it in the host and transfer it to progeny.

key_terms.definition_md: Techniques to alter the chemistry of genetic material and introduce it into host organisms.
Small, circular, autonomously replicating DNA outside the chromosome in bacteria.
DNA sequence where replication begins; it also controls copy number.

visual.alt: Flow of the three basic steps of genetic modification

sections.heading: 2. Restriction enzymes and gel electrophoresis
sections.body_md:
In **1963**, two enzymes restricting bacteriophage growth in *E. coli* were isolated: one added methyl groups to DNA, the other cut it (**restriction endonuclease**). The first, **Hind II**, recognised a specific **six-base-pair** sequence (**recognition sequence**). More than **900** restriction enzymes from over **230** bacterial strains are now known.

**Naming (EcoRI):** E — genus *Escherichia*; co — species *coli*; R — strain RY 13; I — order of isolation. Restriction enzymes belong to **nucleases**: **exonucleases** remove nucleotides from the ends; **endonucleases** cut at specific positions within the DNA.

**Palindromic sequences:** each restriction endonuclease recognises a sequence that reads the same 5′→3′ on both strands, e.g. 5′-GAATTC-3′ / 3′-CTTAAG-5′. EcoRI cuts between G and A on each strand, a little away from the centre, leaving single-stranded overhangs (**sticky ends**) that form hydrogen bonds with complementary ends; **DNA ligase** joins them. Cutting the vector and source DNA with the **same enzyme** gives matching sticky ends.

**Agarose gel electrophoresis:** agarose (from seaweed) acts as a sieve; negatively charged DNA moves towards the **anode**; **smaller fragments move farther**; DNA stained with **ethidium bromide** shows orange bands under **UV**; bands are cut out and the DNA extracted (**elution**).

sections.heading: 3. Cloning vectors and competent hosts
sections.body_md:
**Vector features:**
- **Origin of replication (ori):** starts replication; controls the copy number of linked DNA.
- **Selectable marker:** identifies transformants and eliminates non-transformants — genes for resistance to **ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin**.
- **Cloning sites:** very few, preferably single, recognition sites for commonly used restriction enzymes.
- **Small size.**

**pBR322:** ori, rop, **ampR** and **tetR**; BamHI and SalI sites lie in tetR; PvuI and PstI in ampR. **Insertional inactivation:** an insert in tetR (e.g. at BamHI) makes recombinants **ampicillin-resistant but tetracycline-sensitive**. Alternative: insertion into the **β-galactosidase** gene; with a chromogenic substrate, non-recombinants give **blue** colonies and recombinants **white**.

**Plant and animal vectors:** ***Agrobacterium tumefaciens*** delivers T-DNA into plant cells; its **Ti plasmid** is **disarmed** for use as a vector. **Retroviruses** are disarmed to deliver genes into animal cells.

**Competent hosts:** DNA is hydrophilic and cannot cross membranes. Bacteria are treated with a **divalent cation (calcium)**, incubated on ice with DNA, given a **heat shock (42 °C)** and returned to ice. Other methods: **micro-injection** (into animal cell nucleus), **biolistics / gene gun** (plant cells bombarded with gold or tungsten particles coated with DNA), **disarmed pathogen** vectors.

sections.heading: 4. Processes of recombinant DNA technology
sections.body_md:
1. **Isolation of DNA:** break cells with **lysozyme** (bacteria), **cellulase** (plants) or **chitinase** (fungi); remove RNA with **ribonuclease** and proteins with **protease**; precipitate DNA with **chilled ethanol** (fine threads, spooling).
2. **Cutting:** restriction enzyme; progress checked by agarose gel electrophoresis; vector cut with the same enzyme.
3. **Amplification by PCR:** **denaturation** (high temperature separates strands), **annealing** (two primers bind), **extension** by thermostable **Taq polymerase** from ***Thermus aquaticus***; copies = 2ⁿ after n cycles (about a billion after 30 cycles).
4. **Ligation:** gene joined to vector by **DNA ligase** → recombinant DNA.
5. **Transformation and selection:** recombinant DNA introduced into competent cells; cells grown on antibiotic medium so only transformants survive.
6. **Obtaining the product:** expressed gene gives a **recombinant protein**; large-scale growth in **continuous culture** (cells kept in log phase) in **bioreactors** (100–1000 L) providing optimal temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins and oxygen. **Stirred-tank** bioreactor: curved-base cylinder; stirrer for mixing and oxygen availability; sterile air through a sparger; agitator, oxygen delivery, foam control, temperature and pH control, sampling ports.
7. **Downstream processing:** separation, purification, formulation with preservatives, clinical trials (drugs), strict quality control.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up the parts of the name EcoRI (R is the strain RY 13).
- Saying DNA moves to the cathode, or that larger fragments move farther.
- Saying an insert at BamHI destroys ampicillin resistance (it inactivates tetR).
- Giving the wrong cell-wall enzyme (lysozyme–bacteria, cellulase–plants, chitinase–fungi).
- Forgetting why Taq polymerase is used (it is thermostable).
- Leaving out downstream processing stages.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: term, enzyme, organism, copy number.
- 2–3-mark answers: tool + function + example; steps in correct order.
- 5-mark answers: full sequence of rDNA technology, or vectors with pBR322 and selection, or PCR with a diagram.
- Case-based items: gel results, PCR numbers or selection plates, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: In the name EcoRI, what does “R” stand for?

options.text_md: The species of the bacterium
Restriction
The order in which the enzyme was isolated
The strain of the bacterium (RY 13)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A gene and the vector into which it is to be inserted should be cut with the same restriction enzyme.

**Reason (R):** The same enzyme produces matching sticky ends that can pair and be joined by DNA ligase.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; matching sticky ends are the reason for using the same enzyme — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Foreign DNA is inserted at the BamHI site of pBR322 and the plasmid is put into E. coli. How will the recombinant cells behave?

options.text_md: They grow on tetracycline but not on ampicillin.
They grow on both antibiotics.
They grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline.
They grow on neither antibiotic.

questions.solution_md: The BamHI site lies in the tetracycline-resistance gene, so the insert inactivates it while ampR stays intact — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these double-stranded sequences (top strand shown 5′→3′) could be the recognition site of a restriction endonuclease?

options.text_md: GAATTG
GACGTA
GGATCC
AATTCG

questions.solution_md: Only GGATCC equals its reverse complement (GGATCC), so it reads the same 5′→3′ on both strands — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The first recombinant DNA was made in 1972 by

options.text_md: Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer, using a plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium
Watson and Crick, using bacteriophage DNA
Kary Mullis, using PCR
Alexander Fleming, using Penicillium

questions.solution_md: Cohen and Boyer linked an antibiotic-resistance gene to a native plasmid of Salmonella typhimurium and transferred it into E. coli — option (a).

questions.stem_md: How does a restriction endonuclease differ from an exonuclease?

options.text_md: It joins DNA fragments, whereas an exonuclease cuts them.
It cuts DNA at specific positions within the molecule, whereas an exonuclease removes nucleotides from the ends.
It copies DNA, whereas an exonuclease translates it.
It works only on RNA.

questions.solution_md: Endonucleases cut within DNA at recognition sites; exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A mixture of DNA fragments of 4000 bp, 1500 bp and 300 bp is run on an agarose gel. Which fragment is found farthest from the well?

options.text_md: 300 bp
All travel the same distance

questions.solution_md: The gel acts as a sieve; the smallest fragment moves fastest towards the anode — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? DNA bands in an agarose gel can be seen with the naked eye without any staining.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. DNA is stained with ethidium bromide and seen as bright orange bands under UV light.

questions.stem_md: Why does DNA move towards the anode during gel electrophoresis?

options.text_md: DNA is positively charged because of its bases.
Agarose pushes DNA towards the anode.
DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups.
Ethidium bromide carries DNA to the anode.

questions.solution_md: The phosphate backbone gives DNA a negative charge, so it moves towards the positive electrode (anode) — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Cutting out a separated DNA band from an agarose gel and extracting the DNA from it is called ______.
questions.solution_md: Elution.

questions.stem_md: A gene is joined to a DNA fragment that lacks an origin of replication and is put into E. coli. What is most likely to happen to the gene as the bacteria multiply?

options.text_md: It is copied many times, because all DNA in a cell replicates.
It is not copied, so it is lost from most of the cells as they divide.
It makes the bacteria resistant to all antibiotics.
It is cut out by DNA ligase.

questions.solution_md: Only DNA linked to an ori is replicated; without one, the gene is diluted out as cells divide — option (b).

questions.stem_md: After transformation, a scientist spreads E. coli on a medium containing ampicillin. The vector carries an ampicillin-resistance gene. What does this step achieve?

options.text_md: All cells become recombinant.
Only cells that have taken up the vector survive and form colonies.
The vector is cut open.
Non-transformed cells are converted into transformants.

questions.solution_md: The resistance gene is a selectable marker: untransformed cells die on ampicillin, so transformants are selected — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In blue-white screening, a colony stays white on a medium with a chromogenic substrate. What does this indicate?

options.text_md: The colony has no plasmid at all.
The colony is recombinant: the insert has inactivated the β-galactosidase gene.
The colony contains a non-recombinant plasmid with an active β-galactosidase gene.
The colony is resistant to all antibiotics.

questions.solution_md: An insert inactivates β-galactosidase, so the substrate is not converted into a blue product; the colony stays white — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which bacterium is called a natural genetic engineer of plants because it transfers a piece of its DNA into plant cells?

options.text_md: Agrobacterium tumefaciens
Escherichia coli
Thermus aquaticus
Salmonella typhimurium

questions.solution_md: Agrobacterium tumefaciens transfers T-DNA from its Ti plasmid into plant cells — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Why are bacterial cells treated with calcium ions and given a heat shock before transformation?

options.text_md: To make them competent, so that hydrophilic DNA can enter through the cell wall and membrane
To kill the bacteria before adding DNA
To cut the plasmid open
To make the bacteria resistant to antibiotics

questions.solution_md: DNA cannot pass through membranes; calcium and heat shock make the cells competent to take it up — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A scientist wants to introduce a gene into rice cells without using any bacterial or viral vector. Which method is suitable?

options.text_md: Micro-injection into the nucleus of a bacterium
Treating the rice cells with ethidium bromide
Biolistics: bombarding the cells with gold or tungsten particles coated with the DNA
Running the DNA on an agarose gel

questions.solution_md: The gene gun (biolistics) is suitable for plant cells and needs no vector — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Fragment X was cut out with EcoRI and fragment Y with BamHI. A plasmid was opened with EcoRI. Which fragment can be inserted into the plasmid by DNA ligase most easily, and why?

options.text_md: Y, because BamHI sites are palindromes
Both equally, because ligase joins any ends
X, because its sticky ends match those of the EcoRI-cut plasmid
Neither, because ligase cuts DNA

questions.solution_md: Only fragments cut with the same enzyme have complementary sticky ends that pair before ligation — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A vector carries a kanamycin-resistance gene as its selectable marker. On which medium should transformed cells be grown to select transformants?

Medium containing ethidium bromide
Medium containing lysozyme
Medium containing kanamycin

questions.solution_md: Only cells carrying the vector survive on kanamycin, so transformants are selected — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A scientist wants to introduce a gene directly into the nucleus of a fertilised egg of a cow. Which method is most suitable?

options.text_md: Micro-injection
Biolistics with gold particles
Calcium chloride and heat shock
Agrobacterium-mediated transfer

questions.solution_md: Recombinant DNA is injected directly into the nucleus of animal cells by micro-injection — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A circular plasmid has three recognition sites for an enzyme and is cut completely. How many DNA fragments are produced?
questions.solution_md: A circle has no free ends, so each cut adds one fragment only after the first opens it: number of fragments $= 3$, equal to the number of cuts.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.stem_md: A linear DNA strand 5′–ATGAATTCGGCTAGAATTCTTACGAATTCAG–3′ is digested completely with EcoRI (site GAATTC, cut between G and A). How many fragments are produced?
questions.solution_md: GAATTC occurs 3 times, giving 3 cuts; a linear molecule with 3 cuts gives $3 + 1 = 4$ fragments.

questions.stem_md: A restriction enzyme recognises a four-base sequence. In random DNA, about how many recognition sites would you expect in 8192 base pairs?
questions.solution_md: A four-base site occurs about once in $4^4 = 256$ bases; $\dfrac{8192}{256} = 32$.

options.text_md: Restriction endonuclease

Origin of replication
Selectable marker

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens is used as a cloning vector for plants after it is disarmed.

**Reason (R):** Agrobacterium tumefaciens causes tumours in many dicot plants.

Choose the correct option.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In agarose gel electrophoresis, smaller DNA fragments travel farther than larger ones.

**Reason (R):** The agarose gel acts as a sieve, slowing down larger fragments more.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; the sieving effect explains the separation by size — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Define biotechnology and name its two core techniques.

answer.model_answer_md: Biotechnology is the **integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof and molecular analogues for products and services** (European Federation of Biotechnology). Its two core techniques are **genetic engineering** and **bioprocess engineering** (maintaining a sterile ambience to grow the desired cells in large quantities).

questions.solution_md: Definition and two techniques.

questions.stem_md: Explain how restriction enzymes such as EcoRI are named, using EcoRI as the example.

answer.model_answer_md: The first letter is the **genus** and the next two letters the **species** of the bacterium (**E**scherichia **co**li); the next letter is the **strain** (**R**, from RY 13); the Roman numeral is the **order in which the enzyme was isolated** from that strain (**I** = first).

questions.solution_md: Genus, species, strain, order.

questions.stem_md: The enzyme BamHI recognises the sequence 5′–GGATCC–3′. Write the complementary strand and show that the site is a palindrome. What kind of ends does BamHI leave if it cuts between the two Gs on each strand?

answer.model_answer_md: Complementary strand: **3′–CCTAGG–5′**; read 5′→3′ it is **GGATCC**, the **same** as the top strand, so the site is a **palindrome**. Cutting between G and G on both strands is **staggered**, leaving single-stranded **sticky ends** (GATC overhangs).

questions.solution_md: Reverse complement equals the original; staggered cut gives sticky ends.

questions.stem_md: Why must bacterial cells be made competent before transformation, and how is this done?

answer.model_answer_md: DNA is **hydrophilic** and cannot pass through cell membranes, so bacteria do not take it up easily. The cells are treated with a **divalent cation such as calcium**, which increases the efficiency of DNA entry; they are incubated **on ice** with the recombinant DNA, given a brief **heat shock at 42 °C**, and returned to ice.

questions.solution_md: Hydrophilic DNA; calcium and heat shock.

questions.stem_md: Describe agarose gel electrophoresis and how the separated DNA is seen and recovered.

answer.model_answer_md:
DNA fragments are loaded into wells of an **agarose gel** (agarose comes from seaweed) at the **cathode** end. An electric current is passed; the **negatively charged** DNA moves towards the **anode**. The gel acts as a **sieve**, so **smaller fragments move farther**, separating by size.

The DNA is stained with **ethidium bromide** and seen as **orange bands under UV light**. A band is cut out and its DNA extracted (**elution**) for use in constructing recombinant DNA.

questions.solution_md: Loading, migration by size, staining, elution.

marking_scheme.step: Movement of negatively charged DNA to the anode
Staining with ethidium bromide and elution

questions.stem_md: State three features required in a cloning vector, and explain the role of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Origin of replication (ori):** where replication starts; it also controls the **copy number** of the linked DNA.

2. **Selectable marker:** a gene, usually for **antibiotic resistance** (ampicillin, tetracycline and so on), that helps **identify transformants** and eliminate non-transformants.

3. **Cloning sites:** very few, preferably **single**, recognition sites for common restriction enzymes, so the vector is cut only once and the gene is inserted neatly. (Small size is also useful.)

questions.solution_md: Ori, marker, cloning sites.

questions.stem_md: A student inserts a gene at the BamHI site of pBR322 and transforms E. coli. Describe how she can identify the colonies that contain recombinant plasmids.

answer.model_answer_md: She first plates the cells on **ampicillin**: only cells with a plasmid (recombinant or not) grow, because **ampR** is intact. She then transfers (replica-plates) the colonies onto **tetracycline**. The BamHI site lies in **tetR**, so an insert there **inactivates** it (**insertional inactivation**). Colonies that grow on ampicillin but **fail to grow on tetracycline** are the **recombinants**.

questions.solution_md: Ampicillin then tetracycline; insertional inactivation.

questions.stem_md: Describe the tools of recombinant DNA technology: restriction enzymes, cloning vectors and competent hosts.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Restriction enzymes.** Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific recognition sequences, which are palindromes reading the same 5′→3′ on both strands (for example GAATTC for EcoRI). Many cut the two strands a little away from the centre, leaving sticky ends. The vector and source DNA are cut with the same enzyme so that their sticky ends match and can be joined by DNA ligase. More than 900 such enzymes are known; their names, such as EcoRI, give the genus, species, strain and order of isolation.

**Cloning vectors.** Plasmids and bacteriophages are used. A vector needs an origin of replication, which also controls copy number; a selectable marker such as an ampicillin- or tetracycline-resistance gene; few, preferably single, cloning sites; and small size. In pBR322, inserting DNA into tetR causes insertional inactivation, which identifies recombinants; blue-white screening uses the β-galactosidase gene instead. For plants, the disarmed Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens is used; for animals, disarmed retroviruses.

**Competent hosts.** Because DNA is hydrophilic, bacterial cells are made competent by calcium treatment and a heat shock at 42 °C. Other methods are micro-injection into the nucleus of animal cells and biolistics (gene gun) for plant cells.

questions.stem_md: After transformation, a culture contains three kinds of E. coli cells: without any plasmid, with a non-recombinant plasmid, and with a recombinant plasmid. Explain how antibiotic resistance and insertional inactivation can be used to identify each kind, and compare this with blue-white screening.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Antibiotic selection.** The vector pBR322 carries ampicillin- and tetracycline-resistance genes, and the gene was inserted at the BamHI site inside tetR. On ampicillin medium, cells without a plasmid die, while cells with either kind of plasmid grow, because ampR is intact. The colonies are then replica-plated onto tetracycline. Non-recombinant plasmids still have a working tetR, so their cells grow. In recombinants the insert has inactivated tetR (insertional inactivation), so they do not grow. Thus: no plasmid — no growth on either; non-recombinant — grows on both; recombinant — grows on ampicillin only.

**Blue-white screening.** Here the gene is inserted into the coding sequence of β-galactosidase. On a medium with a chromogenic substrate, non-recombinant colonies, with an active enzyme, turn blue; recombinant colonies, whose enzyme gene is inactivated, stay white.

**Comparison.** Antibiotic selection needs two plates and replica plating; blue-white screening identifies recombinants on a single plate by colour, so it is simpler and faster.

questions.stem_md: Describe, in order, the processes of recombinant DNA technology, from isolating DNA to obtaining the final product.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Isolation of DNA.** Cells are broken open with lysozyme (bacteria), cellulase (plants) or chitinase (fungi). RNA is removed with ribonuclease and proteins with protease, and the DNA is precipitated with chilled ethanol and spooled.

**Cutting.** The DNA is digested with a restriction enzyme, and the digestion is checked by agarose gel electrophoresis. The vector is cut with the same enzyme.

**Amplification.** The gene of interest is amplified by PCR: repeated cycles of denaturation, annealing of primers and extension by thermostable Taq polymerase give about a billion copies after 30 cycles.

**Ligation.** The gene is joined to the cut vector by DNA ligase, making recombinant DNA.

**Transformation and selection.** The recombinant DNA is introduced into competent host cells, which are grown on a medium containing an antibiotic so that only transformants survive; recombinants are identified by insertional inactivation or blue-white screening.

**Product.** The host expresses the gene, producing a recombinant protein. Cells are grown on a large scale in bioreactors, often by continuous culture.

**Downstream processing.** The product is separated, purified, formulated with preservatives and, if a drug, tested in clinical trials and quality control.

answer.model_answer_md:
**PCR.** The polymerase chain reaction copies a chosen region of DNA in a test tube. Each cycle has three steps: denaturation at high temperature separates the strands; annealing lets two primers, short oligonucleotides complementary to the ends of the target, bind; and extension by Taq polymerase copies each strand from the primers.

**Why it works on tiny samples.** Each cycle doubles the number of copies, so after n cycles one molecule becomes 2ⁿ; thirty cycles give about a billion copies, enough for analysis. Taq polymerase, from Thermus aquaticus, is thermostable, so it survives every heating step and the cycles can be run automatically.

**Evaluation.** The trainee is wrong: the amount of starting DNA is not a barrier, because PCR amplifies even a few molecules to large quantities.

**Precaution.** Because PCR amplifies any DNA present, the sample must be protected from contamination (for example, by DNA from the handlers), using clean equipment and controls.

questions.stem_md: Explain how a recombinant protein is produced on a large scale, describing the stirred-tank bioreactor and the stages of downstream processing.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Expression.** When the inserted gene is expressed in host cells, they make a recombinant protein. Small flask cultures give little product, so cells are grown in bioreactors, often by continuous culture, in which used medium is drained out and fresh medium added, keeping cells in their log phase for higher yields.

**Bioreactor.** Bioreactors are large vessels, often 100–1000 litres, that provide optimal temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins and oxygen. The common stirred-tank type is a cylinder with a curved base. A motor-driven stirrer mixes the contents and spreads oxygen; sterile air is bubbled in through a sparger. It has an agitator system, an oxygen-delivery system, foam control, temperature control, pH control and sampling ports for withdrawing small volumes to check the culture.

**Downstream processing.** After biosynthesis, the product is separated from the cells and medium, purified, and formulated with preservatives. Drugs must undergo clinical trials, and all products need strict quality control before marketing.
